units.title: Form 5 VA start: public-exam structure and visual diary
units.intro: This unit starts Form 5 visual arts. You will revisit the two learning strands (appreciation and making), learn how the two public-exam papers are structured, and continue a weekly visual diary. Lessons teach structure and method only. They do not use real public exam papers or high-score student exemplars.

lessons.title: Form 5 start: course review and the two public-exam papers
cards: Form 5 visual arts starts with a review. The two strands are still appreciation and making, and you keep practising both.
The public exam has two papers. You choose Paper 1 or Paper 2. Paper 1 begins with a flat-work requirement; Paper 2 follows the design task as set.
Appreciation practice: describe the forms you see, then note a possible cultural situation. Making practice: choose one medium and try one small step.
Lessons teach structure and method only. They do not use real public exam papers or high-score student exemplars.

quiz.question: What do you do with the two public-exam papers?
options: Hand in both papers at once
Only an oral exam is allowed
quiz.explain: The structure is a choice of one paper.

quiz.question: Paper 1 begins with a requirement for ＿＿ work.
quiz.explain: Paper 1 starts from flat work.

quiz.question: Match each strand to a practice

answer.Making: Try one step in a medium

quiz.explain: Review both strands and the paper structure together.

quiz.question: Order the Form 5 start steps.
quiz.explain: Review, distinguish the papers, note a choice, then keep the diary.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one line on what you notice; right, one making step.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, say how you review appreciation and making together, and how Paper 1 differs from Paper 2. Hint: sentence one names the strands; sentence two names the structural difference.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Weekly visual diary: research and record
cards: A weekly visual diary is a habit of research and record. One page can hold a sketch, one observation, and one open question.
Keep the record in class. Use photos and objects you already have, or materials your teacher provides.
Research can ask: what forms do you see, what might they be for, and which medium will you try next week?
Note the diary gently. This page does not use a real exam paper as a model.

quiz.question: What is a weekly visual diary mainly for?
quiz.explain: The diary serves research and record.

quiz.question: One diary page can hold a sketch, an observation, and one ＿＿.
quiz.explain: An open question carries the work into next week.

quiz.question: Match the diary parts

answer.Observation: One sentence on what you noticed
answer.Materials: Objects or photos already in class

quiz.explain: All three records happen in class.

quiz.question: Order one visual-diary entry.
options: Choose one material in the classroom
Leave one question for next week
quiz.explain: Material, sketch, observation, then a question.

quiz.question: Compare works: left is a sketch page, right is a research question. One note each.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: Use “material + observation + next-week question” to say how you will keep this week’s visual diary. Hint: all three must be possible in class.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

units.title: What is aesthetic: Chinese and Western views, plus Song–Yuan art intro
units.intro: This unit asks how beauty can be understood in Chinese and Western societies, then uses a compact timeline to introduce Song–Yuan art. Practise looking at form, function and cultural context. This is an introduction only, not a complete technique course. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

lessons.title: What is aesthetic: how Chinese and Western societies see beauty
cards: Beauty can be understood differently in Chinese and Western societies. One view may stress harmony and character; another may stress personal feeling or experiments with form.
In practice, separate three things: form (what you see), function (what it is for), and cultural context (the kind of life it belongs to).
This lesson does not call one society the correct one. You should be able to name the angle you are using.
This is an introduction only, not a complete technique course. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: How does this lesson ask you to look at beauty?
options: Separate form, function, and cultural context
Copy one famous painting to finish
quiz.answer: Separate form, function, and cultural context
quiz.explain: The three angles make your view of beauty clear.

quiz.question: Cultural context means the kind of ＿＿ a work belongs to.
quiz.explain: Context is about life and culture, not price.

quiz.question: Match the three angles
quiz.explain: Use all three angles together.

quiz.question: Order one observation of beauty.
options: Name the angle you are using
quiz.explain: From what you see, to use, to context and angle.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one line on form; right, one line on cultural context. Do not call either side the correct society.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In three sentences, show how one classroom object has form, function, and cultural context. Hint: one angle per sentence.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: An introduction to Song–Yuan art
cards: The Song–Yuan introduction uses a compact timeline: learn a rough order first, then look at form in one work.
Song and Yuan can sit side by side. Court, literati, and popular visual choices can differ. Name the point you are comparing.
A timeline is not a list of every year to memorise. For an introduction, place one work roughly, then describe form and function.
This is an introduction only, not a complete technique course. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: What is the Song–Yuan timeline mainly for?
options: Placing a work in a rough order
Copying one famous painting in full
quiz.answer: Placing a work in a rough order
quiz.explain: A compact timeline is a rough place, not every date.

quiz.question: Before comparing Song and Yuan, name the ＿＿ you are comparing.
quiz.explain: A comparison needs one clear point.

quiz.question: Match the introduction steps

answer.Function: What the work might be for

quiz.explain: Order, form, and function are enough for an introduction.

quiz.question: Order a Song–Yuan introduction.
quiz.explain: From the timeline to one work’s form and function.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one formal note on Song; right, one formal note on Yuan. Name the point you compare.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, place one Song or Yuan work on the compact timeline. Hint: sentence one is the rough place; sentence two is one form and one function.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

units.title: Self, heritage and society
units.intro: This unit starts from how tradition and society shape everyday life. Practise gathering material in a visual journal, developing a theme, and testing ideas in ink and mixed media. You will compare methods in strange-stone images with Surrealism and Cubism, rather than copying a picture. Interviews, observation and collecting stay as classroom practice. Lessons do not use high-score exemplars.

lessons.title: How tradition and society shape everyday life
cards: Tradition and society reach you through everyday objects, festival colours, and how things are arranged at home.
Start from one everyday object: its form, its place in daily life, and your own response.
Interviews, observation, and collecting stay as classroom practice. A conversation, a photo you already have, or a classroom object is enough.
Lessons do not use high-score exemplars. Write the influence you actually see.

quiz.question: Where does this lesson ask you to start?
options: A famous painting you must copy
quiz.explain: Start from an object in everyday life.

quiz.question: Interviews, observation, and collecting stay as ＿＿ practice.
quiz.explain: All three stay in the classroom.

quiz.question: Match everyday influences

answer.Your response: How you feel it affects you

quiz.explain: All three together show an influence.

quiz.question: Order one everyday observation.
options: Note its place in daily life
quiz.explain: Object, form, place, then response.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, the object’s form; right, its place in daily life.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In three sentences, show how tradition or society shapes one everyday object for you. Hint: one sentence each for form, place, and response, all possible in class.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Strange-stone comparison: Wu Bin with Surrealism and Cubism
cards: Strange-stone comparison is about method, not copying a picture. Look at how Wu Bin makes a rock strange, then at how Surrealism and Cubism reassemble what is seen.
A comparison can ask: where is it exaggerated, where is it cut apart, and where can you still tell it is stone?
Surrealism often puts unusual combinations together. Cubism often breaks an object into many faces. Talk about the method, not about copying one painting.
Images stay as classroom diagrams. Lessons do not use high-score exemplars.

quiz.question: What does the strange-stone comparison ask you to do?
options: Compare methods rather than copy a picture
quiz.answer: Compare methods rather than copy a picture
quiz.explain: The comparison is about method, not copying.

quiz.question: Cubism often breaks an object into many ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Many faces describes a formal method.

quiz.question: Match the methods

answer.Wu Bin’s strange stones: Make the rock strange and still readable as stone
answer.Cubism: Break an object into many faces

quiz.explain: All three are methods, not pictures to copy.

quiz.question: Order one strange-stone comparison.
options: Point to exaggeration or a cut
Name one Surrealist or Cubist method
Write one step you would try
quiz.explain: From what you see, to a method, to one step of your own.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one method in Wu Bin’s strange stones; right, one Surrealist or Cubist method. Do not copy a picture.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, compare Wu Bin with Surrealism or Cubism. Hint: sentence one is the stone’s form; sentence two is a method, and you say you are not copying a picture.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Visual journal: how to gather material and develop a theme
cards: A visual journal gathers material and develops a theme. One page collects; a later page narrows.
Gathering can be a classroom sketch, a photo you already have, a short interview note, or one collected object.
To develop a theme, pick an interest that keeps returning in the material, then write it as one sentence.
Interviews, observation, and collecting stay as classroom practice. Lessons do not use high-score exemplars.

quiz.question: What does the journal do before a theme is developed?
options: Hand in a real exam paper
quiz.explain: Gather first, then narrow to a theme.

quiz.question: A theme sentence comes from an ＿＿ that keeps returning in the material.
quiz.explain: A returning interest is what becomes the theme.

quiz.question: Match gathering and developing

answer.Theme sentence: One sentence from a returning interest

quiz.explain: Gathering and the theme both happen in class.

quiz.question: Order gathering and developing.
options: Decide what the next page will try
quiz.explain: Material, interest, theme, then a next step.

quiz.question: Compare works: left is a gathering page, right is a theme sentence. Note what you see and what you narrowed.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: Use “two materials + one theme sentence” to show how you move from gathering to developing. Hint: the materials must be possible in class.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Ink experiments and the first portfolio piece
cards: Ink experiments try a few small effects with ink, water, and paper, then you choose one that fits your theme.
The first portfolio piece uses a research and making structure: one theme sentence, material evidence, one medium test, and a next step.
Mixed media can be tested with ink. Change only one condition at a time so you can record the difference.
Lessons do not use high-score exemplars. You show your own test and structure, not a real exam paper.

quiz.question: Which item belongs in the first portfolio piece?
options: The full text of a real exam paper
A theme sentence and one medium test
quiz.answer: A theme sentence and one medium test
quiz.explain: The first piece uses theme, evidence, a test, and a next step.

quiz.question: Each mixed-media test changes only one ＿＿.
quiz.explain: One change at a time makes the comparison clear.

quiz.question: Match the first-piece structure

answer.Next step: What you want to try next

quiz.explain: The three parts together make the structure.

quiz.question: Order the ink test and the first portfolio piece.
quiz.explain: Theme, test, record, then next step.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one ink effect; right, the theme sentence of the first portfolio piece.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: Use “theme sentence + one test + next step” for the first portfolio piece. Hint: name the condition you changed, and do not use a high-score exemplar.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

units.title: Traditional symbols, colour and pattern
units.intro: This unit looks at signs and symbols in traditional colour, pattern and painting, then continues Song–Yuan observation. Practise describing the forms you see and the meanings they might carry. All of it happens in class.

lessons.title: Signs and symbols in traditional colour, pattern and painting
cards: Traditional colour, pattern, and painting can carry signs. The same colour can mean different things in different lives.
Separate the form you see from a meaning you suggest. Write the meaning as “might”, not as the only answer.
Pattern can be repetition, symmetry, or an object used again and again. Name which kind of repeat you see.
All of it happens in class. A classroom diagram and your own description are enough.

quiz.question: How should you write a symbolic meaning?
options: As a meaning it might carry
quiz.answer: As a meaning it might carry
quiz.explain: A symbol is a possible meaning, not the only one.

quiz.question: Pattern can be repetition, symmetry, or an object used ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Using something again and again is one kind of pattern.

quiz.question: Match symbol study

answer.Meaning: A meaning the form might carry

quiz.explain: Form first, then a possible meaning.

quiz.question: Order one symbol description.
options: Point to a colour or pattern
Say that this is a suggestion
quiz.explain: From the form you see to a possible meaning.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, form only; right, one possible meaning.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, describe one traditional colour or pattern. Hint: sentence one is form only; sentence two uses “might” for the meaning.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Song–Yuan art, continued
cards: Song–Yuan art, continued, means choosing one more formal detail after the introduction.
Compare one similarity and one difference, such as empty space, the density of lines, or the proportion of figures to landscape.
The continuation is still observation. It is not a full technique course, and it is not copying a whole famous painting.
All of it happens in class. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: What does the Song–Yuan continuation mainly add?
options: Hand in a real exam paper
quiz.explain: The continuation is one more look at form.

quiz.question: When comparing two works, write one similarity and one ＿＿.
quiz.explain: A comparison needs a similarity and a difference.

quiz.question: Match the continued look

answer.Density: Where lines are dense or open
answer.Proportion: Whether figures or landscape take more space

quiz.explain: All three are formal details.

quiz.question: Order one continued comparison.
quiz.explain: Choose the works and the detail, then similarity and difference.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one shared form; right, one different form.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, continue one Song–Yuan observation. Hint: sentence one is a formal detail; sentence two is a similarity or a difference.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

units.title: Role-taking: re-presenting a person in a Chinese context
units.intro: This unit practises role-taking: how to re-present a person in a Chinese context. You will try wet and dry media, and use research and making structures to develop the second portfolio piece. Lessons do not use high-score student exemplars.

lessons.title: Role and identity: how to re-present a person
cards: Role-taking asks how a person can be re-presented: identity, clothing, pose, and how a viewer might read them.
Re-presenting in a Chinese context may borrow a traditional pose, sign, or setting. Say what you borrowed and what you changed.
A role is not a likeness contest. Write what the person is doing in the picture, and which detail carries identity.
Lessons do not use high-score student exemplars. Use the method and your own sentences.

quiz.question: When you re-present a person, what matters most to say?
quiz.explain: The practice is about how identity is shown.

quiz.question: After borrowing a traditional pose, write what you ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Name both the borrowing and the change.

quiz.question: Match role elements

answer.Identity: What kind of role the person is

quiz.explain: All three together re-present a person.

quiz.question: Order one role-taking practice.
options: Choose one detail from a Chinese context
quiz.explain: Person, identity, detail, then the change.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, a pose or sign you borrow; right, what you change.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, say how you re-present a person in a Chinese context. Hint: sentence one is identity and pose; sentence two is one detail and what you change.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Wet and dry media experiments
cards: Dry media such as pencil, pastel, and charcoal often keep a clear edge. Wet media such as ink and watercolour spread.
In a test, change one condition: dry or wet, light or heavy pressure, or whether the paper is damp.
Record what you used, the effect you saw, and whether that effect could serve the clothing or the setting of a role.
Try it all in class. Lessons do not use high-score student exemplars.

quiz.question: One clear difference between wet and dry media is?
options: Wet media are always more correct
Dry media cannot make a line
You must finish both at the same time
quiz.explain: Wet media spread; dry media keep an edge more easily.

quiz.question: Each test changes only one ＿＿.
quiz.explain: One condition at a time shows the difference.

quiz.question: Match medium and effect

answer.Pencil or charcoal: A clear edge is easier to keep
answer.Record: Write what you used and what you saw

quiz.explain: The test and the record work together.

quiz.question: Order one wet-and-dry test.
options: Watch the edge or the spread
Note whether it can serve the role
quiz.explain: Choice, test, observation, then use.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one dry-media effect; right, one wet-media effect.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, record one wet-and-dry test. Hint: sentence one names the medium and the condition you changed; sentence two says whether the effect can serve the role.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Song–Yuan art and the second portfolio piece
cards: This lesson brings a Song–Yuan observation into the second portfolio piece. You still describe one formal detail, then use it to develop a role or a picture.
The second piece uses research and making: one theme sentence, one piece of research evidence, one dry or wet test, and a next step.
A Song–Yuan detail might be empty space, line, or figure proportion. Borrow the method. Do not copy a whole picture.
Lessons do not use high-score student exemplars or real exam papers.

quiz.question: What does the second portfolio piece connect to?
options: One Song–Yuan formal detail and your role
quiz.answer: One Song–Yuan formal detail and your role
quiz.explain: The second piece joins a Song–Yuan observation to your own structure.

quiz.question: The second piece needs a theme sentence, research evidence, one medium test, and a ＿＿.
quiz.explain: A next step keeps the portfolio moving.

quiz.question: Match the second piece
quiz.explain: The three items serve the second piece.

quiz.question: Order the second piece.
quiz.explain: Theme, detail, test, then next step.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one Song–Yuan formal detail; right, how it enters the second piece.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: Use “theme sentence + one Song–Yuan detail + next step” for the second portfolio piece. Hint: say you borrow a method and do not copy a whole picture.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

units.title: Contemporary China and innovative heritage
units.intro: This unit introduces Xu Bing and contemporary Chinese calligraphy, plus a first look at global contemporary art, then practises innovative heritage through three-dimensional collage and installation. All of it happens in class. It also closes the Song–Yuan observation thread.

lessons.title: Xu Bing and contemporary Chinese calligraphy
cards: Xu Bing and contemporary Chinese calligraphy are studied in class. You look at how writing becomes a visual form.
Ask: can the writing still be read, how are strokes repeated or reassembled, and how is a viewer asked to look?
This lesson stays in class. Classroom writing, a diagram, and your own sentences are enough.
You study the method. You do not copy one artwork’s picture. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: What do you do when you study Xu Bing and contemporary calligraphy?
options: You can learn it only by leaving class
In class, see how writing becomes visual form
quiz.answer: In class, see how writing becomes visual form
quiz.explain: The study stays in class and stays with method.

quiz.question: A contemporary-calligraphy question can ask whether the writing can still be ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Whether it can be read is a visual question.

quiz.question: Match calligraphy looking

answer.Writing: Whether it can still be read
answer.Strokes: How they are repeated or reassembled
answer.Viewer: How they are invited to look

quiz.explain: All three questions are answered in class.

quiz.question: Order one in-class study.
options: Ask whether it can still be read
Write one step you would try
quiz.explain: From looking, to method, to one step of your own.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, whether the writing can still be read; right, how strokes are reassembled. This stays in class.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, describe one method in Xu Bing or contemporary calligraphy. Hint: sentence one links writing and visual form; sentence two is a step you can try in class.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: An introduction to global contemporary art
cards: An introduction to global contemporary art is one comparison. Choose a classroom diagram and ask how its form speaks to a viewer.
A comparison can ask: is the material an everyday object, do you need to move closer to see it whole, and does a title change your reading?
An introduction is not a survey of every region. Be clear about one work’s form and one way of looking.
All of it happens in class. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: What does the global contemporary introduction ask of you?
options: Be clear about one work’s form and one way of looking
Hand in a real exam paper
quiz.answer: Be clear about one work’s form and one way of looking
quiz.explain: The introduction is one work and one method.

quiz.question: A comparison can ask whether a title changes your ＿＿.
quiz.explain: A title can change how you read the form.

quiz.question: Match contemporary looking

answer.Material: Whether it is an everyday object
answer.Distance: Whether you move closer to see it whole
answer.Title: Whether it changes your reading

quiz.explain: All three are ways of looking.

quiz.question: Order one contemporary introduction.
options: Ask about one way of looking
Note whether a title changes the reading
quiz.explain: Diagram, form, way of looking, then title.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, form; right, one way of looking.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, make one introduction to global contemporary art. Hint: sentence one is form; sentence two is how a viewer is invited to look. Keep it in class.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Innovative heritage: three-dimensional collage and installation
cards: Innovative heritage turns a sign or a writing method you have studied into a classroom piece you can walk around: a three-dimensional collage or an installation.
Xu Bing’s approach to writing can be a conceptual reference: can the writing be read, and can parts be reassembled? You do not copy one artwork.
In a three-dimensional collage, add one material at a time and note which viewing angle it changes.
All of it happens in class. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: What does the innovative-heritage lesson mainly try?
options: It can be done only by leaving class
Hand in a real exam paper
quiz.explain: Collage and installation stay in class.

quiz.question: Each three-dimensional collage adds only one ＿＿.
quiz.explain: One material at a time shows which angle changed.

quiz.question: Match innovative heritage

answer.Conceptual reference: Whether writing can be read and parts reassembled
answer.Collage: Add one material at a time
answer.Installation: Move closer to see it whole

quiz.explain: All three are classroom methods.

quiz.question: Order one three-dimensional collage.
options: Choose a sign or a writing method
Move closer and note a new angle
Note that you did not copy an artwork
quiz.explain: Method, material, angle, and not copying an artwork.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, the writing method you refer to; right, the one material you add.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, describe your collage or installation. Hint: sentence one is a sign or writing method; sentence two is one material and one viewing angle. Say you are not copying an artwork.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

lessons.title: Song–Yuan art, closing look
cards: The closing look returns to one form you observed this year: empty space, line, proportion, or one difference among court, literati, and popular work.
Closing is not another memorised timeline. Write one detail into your research workbook and say how it helps your making.
The research workbook runs through the learning. Theme, evidence, a test, and a reflection can sit on one page.
All of it happens in class. Lessons do not use real exam papers.

quiz.question: What does the Song–Yuan closing look mainly do?
options: Memorise the full date list again
Write one formal detail into the research workbook
Hand in a real exam paper
quiz.answer: Write one formal detail into the research workbook
quiz.explain: Closing puts the observation into the workbook.

quiz.question: One workbook page can hold a theme, evidence, a test, and a ＿＿.
quiz.explain: Reflection shows how the detail serves making.

quiz.question: Match the closing page

answer.Workbook: Holds the theme and the evidence

quiz.explain: The three items close the Song–Yuan thread into your own learning.

quiz.question: Order the Song–Yuan closing look.
options: Choose one form you observed this year
Write it into the research workbook
Say how it helps your making
quiz.explain: Detail, workbook, making, then reflection.

quiz.question: Compare works: left, one Song–Yuan formal detail; right, how it helps making in the workbook.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

quiz.question: In two sentences, close the Song–Yuan observation. Hint: sentence one is one formal detail; sentence two says how it enters the research workbook and helps making.
quiz.explain: Practice structure · lessons do not use a real exam paper

units.title: Portfolio review and year reflection
units.intro: This unit practises reviewing a year of learning: what went well, what can improve, and how to write a short portfolio overview. Lessons do not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars.

lessons.title: How to review your strengths and next steps
cards: A review looks at your year: which practice feels steady, and which step is still messy.
A strength needs one piece of evidence: a diary page, one ink test, or a theme sentence you wrote clearly.
The next step is one small action you can do in class. Do not turn it into a submission timetable.
Lessons do not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars. You review your own process.

quiz.question: What must a strength in the review include?
options: One piece of your own evidence
quiz.answer: One piece of your own evidence
quiz.explain: A strength needs your own evidence.

quiz.question: The next step is one small ＿＿ you can do in class.
quiz.explain: One doable step is enough.

quiz.question: Match the review

answer.Evidence: A diary page, a test, or a theme sentence

quiz.explain: The three items make a full review.

quiz.question: Order one self-review.
options: Choose a practice that feels steady
Name one step that is still messy
quiz.explain: Strength, evidence, a weak step, then an action.

lessons.title: Structure for a portfolio overview
cards: A portfolio overview uses four moves: one theme sentence, what the research workbook did, what the artwork or critical study shows, and the next step.
The research workbook and the artwork or critical study are the two parts of the portfolio. The overview says how they support each other.
This lesson does not lock a word count. Keep the four moves, and let each sentence do one job.
Lessons do not use real exam papers or high-score exemplars. The overview is your own structure.
